findings.title: NPE risk when all-clients resource is missing
findings.body: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when there is no resource for the specific client, the code falls back to loading the type-level resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...). That method can return null (e.g., when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false, the type is unknown, or no resource has been created for the type yet). The subsequent authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty() call then dereferences a null resource and throws NullPointerException. The code should guard against a null 'resource' before passing it to findByResource, returning false instead.

findings.title: getClientsWithPermission can return the resource type name as a client id
findings.body: ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission iterates all resources whose type is 'Clients' and adds resource.getName() to the returned set for each resource the admin has the scope on. This includes the 'all-clients' resource whose name is the literal string 'Clients' (set in AdminPermissionsSchema.init). So when an admin has the scope for all clients, the returned set contains the entry 'Clients', which is not a client internal id. Callers expecting a Set<String> of client ids will then attempt to look up a client with id 'Clients' and fail. The method should skip the type-level resource (or filter its name) so only actual client ids end up in the set.

findings.title: Listener no longer cleans up authz data for V2-only realms
findings.body: The event listener for RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent is now wrapped in a check for Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V1 feature). For realms that enable only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2, the listener never runs at all, so on client/role/group removal no cleanup of the corresponding resources in the admin-permissions client occurs. Resources representing deleted clients (and any scope-based policies referencing them) become orphans in the authorization store. The change is needed to avoid UnsupportedOperationException from ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, but the V2 side does not implement equivalent cleanup, so data integrity is now degraded. Either a V2 path that deletes the orphaned resources in the admin permissions client should be added, or the wrapper should also include the V2 feature and dispatch to a V2 cleanup.

findings.title: canMapRoles / canMapCompositeRoles / canMapClientScopeRoles skip the admin-role check
findings.body: Other V2 overrides such as canManage(ClientModel) and canManageClientScopes() first short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS), then fall back to the schema permission. canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission(client, ...) and never consult the admin roles. As a result, a caller that holds the MANAGE_CLIENTS realm role can manage/configure/view a client (and the V2 canView chains through canConfigure which calls canManage) but cannot map roles on it. This is inconsistent with the rest of the V2 evaluators and may surprise administrators; verify whether the V1 canMapRoles also gated on the admin role and, if so, restore the hasOneAdminRole short-circuit.

findings.title: Unused imports, unused logger, and dead private method
findings.body: ClientPermissionsV2 imports org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope (line 27) and the static AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE (line 46) but neither symbol is referenced anywhere in the file. It also declares 'private static final Logger logger = Logger.getLogger(ClientPermissionsV2.class);' (line 51) and a private getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) method (lines 262-272) which is never called. These should be removed to keep the new file clean; if getEvaluationContext is intended for later use it should be marked as such or actually wired into the permission evaluation.

findings.title: Mixed JUnit 4 / JUnit 5 imports in same test
findings.body: PermissionClientTest imports 'static org.junit.Assert.fail' (JUnit 4) while every other fgap test in this PR (e.g. UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest) imports 'static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.fail' (JUnit 5), and the rest of PermissionClientTest already uses JUnit 5 annotations (@Test, @AfterEach from org.junit.jupiter.api). The mixed import is inconsistent and can lead to confusing failure signatures if the wrong Assert is ever picked up; switch to org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.fail to match the surrounding test suite.
